hints: One gas gives a white precipitate with limewater, so identify that gas first, then work out what atoms are left for the second gas and the solid residue.
walkthrough:
Spot the familiar gas from the limewater test**
Think with me about that observation. A white precipitate with saturated calcium hydroxide solution is the classic test for $\text{CO}_{2}$. So one of the two gases must be $\text{CO}_{2}$. The solid left behind is given as $\text{MgO}$.

Balance the remaining C and O atoms**
Start with $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ going to $\text{MgO} + \text{CO}_{2}$. Count atoms: left has $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$, right so far has $\text{C}_{1}\text{O}_{3}$. You are missing one C and one O, which is exactly $\text{CO}$. That gives $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{CO}$, which is fully balanced.

hints: Compare the $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ ions. They have the same charge, so focus on how their ionic radii differ and what that means for charge density.
Link the more strongly polarising cation to distortion of the $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$ anion and why that makes decomposition easier.
walkthrough:
Picture what the cation does to the anion**
Imagine the $2+$ cation sitting next to the large ethanedioate anion, $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$. A very small, highly charging cation pulls electron density out of the anion toward itself. This is polarisation, and it weakens the C-C and C-O bonds inside the anion so less heat is needed to break it apart.

Compare $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$**
Both ions carry the same $2+$ charge, but $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is higher up Group 2, so it is significantly smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$. Smaller radius with the same charge means higher charge density and greater polarising power for $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

Conclude the stability trend**
Because $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ distorts the $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$ ion more strongly, the anion is destabilised more and breaks down more easily. Therefore $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ decomposes at a lower temperature than $\text{CaC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$. This is the same reason Group 2 carbonates become more thermally stable down the group.

Final answer: $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ decomposes at a lower temperature.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, so $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ more strongly polarises / distorts the $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$ anion, weakening bonds within the anion.

hints: Start from the titration data to find moles of $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ used, remembering to convert $\text{cm}^{3}$ to $\text{dm}^{3}$ with $n = c \times V$.
Use the given equation $5\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-} : 2\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ to scale up to moles of $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$ in the $40.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$ sample.
Relate moles of $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$ to moles of $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ (1:1) and divide by the sample volume in $\text{dm}^{3}$ to get solubility in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Find moles of manganate(VII) actually added**
You know concentration times volume gives moles. Convert volumes first: $27.05 \text{ cm}^{3} = 0.02705 \text{ dm}^{3}$. Then:
$$n(\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}) = c \times V = 0.00200 \times 0.02705 = 5.41 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$$

Use the redox ratio to find moles of ethanedioate**
Look at the equation: $5\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-} + 2\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 16\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow 10\text{CO}_{2} + 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. So $2$ mol $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ react with $5$ mol $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$:
$$n(\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}) = 5.41 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{5}{2} = 1.3525 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
This is the amount present in the $40.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$ sample.

Convert to solubility of $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$**
Each $\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}$ releases one $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-}$, so $n(\text{MgC}_{2}\text{O}_{4}) = 1.3525 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$ in $0.0400 \text{ dm}^{3}$. Solubility is just the concentration of the saturated solution:
$$\text{solubility} = \frac{1.3525 \times 10^{-4}}{0.0400} = 3.38 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

Final answer: moles $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} = 0.00200 \times (27.05/1000) = 5.41 \times 10^{-5}$ mol
moles $\text{C}_{2}\text{O}_{4}^{2-} = 5.41 \times 10^{-5} \times 5/2 = 1.35 \times 10^{-4}$ mol in $40.0 \text{ cm}^{3}$
solubility $= 1.3525 \times 10^{-4} / 0.0400 = 3.38 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
